content: Essiac, also known as Essiac Tea, is a blend of herbs used to prepare a tea that some believe possesses cancer-treating properties, though this claim is met with skepticism by others. The formula was discovered by a Canadian nurse named Rene Caisse, who named it after her last name spelled backward. The original recipe is thought to have origins in traditional medicine of the Canadian Ojibwa people and includes greater burdock root (Arctium lappa), slippery elm inner bark (Ulmus rubra, formerly Ulmus fulva), sheep sorrel (Rumex acetosella), and Indian or Turkish rhubarb root (Rheum officinale). According to the National Institutes of Health's Medline, as of early 2008, there is insufficient evidence to either recommend or oppose the use of this herbal mixture as a treatment for any type of cancer. Different brands of Essiac may contain varying ingredients, and the comparative effectiveness of these formulations remains unknown. None of the individual herbs in Essiac have undergone rigorous human cancer trials. While rhubarb has demonstrated some anti-tumor properties in animal studies, slippery elm inner bark has not shown such effects. Sheep sorrel and burdock have been traditionally used in cancer remedies, but their efficacy has not been scientifically validated. Numerous patient testimonials and manufacturer reports are available online, but these cannot be considered scientifically reliable evidence. Cancer patients are advised not to delay treatment with more proven therapies. Rene Caisse operated a free clinic in Bracebridge, Ontario, from 1934 to 1942. During this time, several petitions were submitted to the Ontario Legislature in 1938, requesting that she be allowed to practice throughout the province, but this permission was not granted. Medline notes that there are now over 40 different Essiac-like products being sold in North America, Europe, and Australia. One alternative preparation includes eight herbs, adding red clover (Trifolium pratense), watercress (Nasturtium officinale), blessed thistle (Cnicus benedictus), and kelp (Laminaria digitata) to the original four ingredients. Other formulations incorporate echinacea, black walnut (Juglans nigra), or additional ingredients such as cat's claw (Uncaria tomentosa). Based on tradition, some individuals consume Essiac tea occasionally for general health purposes, detoxification, or to address various ailments other than cancer. These conditions include AIDS, asthma, chronic fatigue syndrome, diabetes, immune system disorders, liver problems, Lyme disease, and lupus erythematosus. However, according to the NIH's Medline, there is even less evidence supporting these applications than there is for cancer treatment. A study on Essiac was initiated with the understanding that Resperin, a company involved in its distribution, would coordinate a scientific trial in humans. However, the study was terminated prematurely due to concerns about improper preparation of the formula and inadequate study design. This research was never completed. Essiac products are currently distributed through Essiac International.
